all.where: Visual 3 ("Of every $100 charged...") — series label "Anthropic inference gross margin", sublabel "deducts all inference infrastructure", and note ("all inference infrastructure (72)")
all.why_opaque: Never defined anywhere in the section, and the everyday English meaning actively misleads: a general reader takes "inference" to mean drawing a conclusion, so "inference infrastructure" reads as nonsense. Worse, the points already teach this exact concept under a different word ("serving"), so the reader has no way to know the middle bar is measuring the same activity T1 and T2 described. The whole descent-of-margins argument in that note depends on recognising it.
all.fix: Attach the name where the concept is already glossed, in T1: "Serving the model — the industry word is inference — works the other way: that cost grows with each answer." Then "inference infrastructure" in Visual 3 lands.

all.where: First named in Visual 1 note ("Marginal cost to serve is about 15% of the US list price") and series label "Marginal cost to serve"; defined only later, in Visual 3's note ("a MARGINAL cost — one more answer on a machine that is already busy")
all.why_opaque: The definition arrives two visuals after first use. Until then the reader is on their own, and colloquial "marginal" means slight, minor, or borderline — so "marginal cost to serve" is naturally misread as "a small cost", which is a conclusion, not a definition. This is the load-bearing term of the entire chapter and of the 7x headline. (The section's own plain_check claims the points define it; they define the idea in T1 but never attach the name.)
all.fix: Name it in T1 where the idea is already explained: "Serving the model works the other way: that cost grows with each answer — a marginal cost, what one more answer costs." Visual 3's fuller contrast with average cost then reinforces rather than rescues.

all.where: First used in T2 ("Serving one token costs about 15% of the US list price"), again in T3/T4 ("$15 per million tokens") and T5; defined only in T6 ("A token is a chunk of text, a bit under a word")
all.why_opaque: Defined four points too late. A reader meets a per-token price, a per-million-token price and two chart units before being told what a token is, so the two most quantitative claims in the section (15% of list, $15 per million) are priced in an unknown unit. Nothing in T2's sentence signals that the word will be explained later.
all.fix: Move a compressed gloss to first use in T2: "Serving one token (a chunk of text, a bit under a word) costs about 15% of the US list price." Keep T6 as is — its point is the deeper one, that token counts differ per job.

all.where: Visual 4 note ("before releasing the weights and while it was the only host") and series sublabel "China, open-weight, sole host at launch"; related "the same open model" in T3/T4
all.why_opaque: "Weights" is deep AI jargon — the trained parameter file that IS the model. A reader with no background cannot guess it, and Visual 4's entire logic is a before/after on that event: Kimi K3 priced at the US rate *while it was still the only host, before the weights shipped*. Miss what releasing weights means and the near-controlled experiment collapses into an unexplained coincidence of two $15 prices.
all.fix: Gloss once at first use in T3/T4: "When many firms can host the same open model — one whose trained file is published, so anyone can run it — price drifts down toward cost." Visual 4's "before releasing the weights" then reads correctly.

all.where: Visual 3 series sublabel "deducts everything in cost of revenue (company-wide)" and note ("then everything in cost of revenue (42.6)")
all.why_opaque: An accounting line item presented as if it were plain English. "Everything in cost of revenue" tells the reader there is a defined boundary but not where it sits, which is precisely the variable the chart is manipulating — the note's whole finding is that the margin thins as the cost boundary widens. Without knowing what falls inside the line, the third bar is just a smaller number.
all.fix: One clause in the sublabel: "deducts everything in cost of revenue (every direct cost of delivering the service, not just chips)".

all.where: Visual 2 series label "DeepSeek real GPU fleet (capex)"; then Visual 7 unit "$ billions, 2026 capex (Big-4 hyperscalers)" and label "Big-4 hyperscaler capex"
all.why_opaque: A finance contraction of "capital expenditure" that is never expanded at first use. Visual 7's note says "capital spending", but that is five visuals later and the two words are never equated. The parenthetical in Visual 2 is doing real work — it flags that the $1.4B is hardware bought up front rather than the training bill — and that distinction is invisible to a reader who cannot decode the word.
all.fix: Expand at first use in Visual 2's note: "The GPU fleet behind it cost an estimated $1.4B — capex, money sunk into hardware before a single answer is sold — about 250x the headline."

all.where: First use in T2 ("SemiAnalysis puts Anthropic's serving margin near 72%"); then Visual 3 unit "% gross margin" and labels "Implied marginal serving margin", "Anthropic inference gross margin", "OpenAI 2025 gross margin"
all.why_opaque: Visual 3's title ("Of every $100 charged, how much is left after cost?") is an excellent plain gloss, but it arrives after T2 has already asserted a bare "serving margin near 72%". At that point the reader has no anchor for what the percentage is a percentage of, and "margin" in ordinary use means an edge or a spare allowance. T1's "keeps about 43 cents of each sales dollar" is the right idiom and is never connected to the word.
all.fix: One clause in T2: "SemiAnalysis puts Anthropic's serving margin — what is left of each sales dollar after the cost of answering — near 72%."

all.where: First use in T2 ("about 15% of the US list price"); Visual 1 unit, note and label; Visual 4 sublabel "US list price, same rate"; Visual 5 note ("would still clear its costs several times over at list") and sublabel "if every token were billed at R1 list price"
all.why_opaque: Visual 1's sublabel "what OpenAI/Anthropic charge" is a partial gloss that arrives after T2 and misses the part that matters: list price is the posted rate before volume discounts and before free users. That is exactly what Visual 5's caveat turns on ("real revenue was far lower because much use was free"), and "at list" there is bare trade shorthand a general reader will not parse as an adverbial phrase at all.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in T2: "...costs about 15% of the US list price, the posted rate before discounts." And in Visual 5's note write "at its posted list price" instead of "at list".

all.term: input price / input tokens vs output tokens
all.where: T5 ("OpenAI's top input price rose from $1.25 to $5.00"); Visual 6 unit "$ per million input tokens" and note; Visual 4 unit "$ per million output tokens"
all.why_opaque: The section never says that these services meter two different things — the text you send in and the text the model writes back — at two different prices. A reader who has just been told a token is a chunk of text will read Visual 4's $15 and Visual 6's $5 as the same quantity and conclude the numbers contradict each other, or that OpenAI is three times cheaper than Anthropic. The confusion is manufactured by placing the two charts in the same section.
all.fix: One clause at first use in T5: "OpenAI's top input price — what it charges for the text you send in, billed separately from the text it writes back — rose from $1.25 to $5.00 in a year."

all.where: Visual 1 note: "Marginal cost to serve is about 15% of the US list price (80% range 6%-48%)"
all.why_opaque: This is the page's first appearance of an uncertainty interval and nothing explains what "80%" qualifies. A reader will guess it means 80% of something in the data rather than a confidence level, and the design intends error bars to be the emotional payload of the whole piece — the reader is asked to read every mark this way from here on. A range of 6% to 48% around a headline of 15% is also startling enough that it needs a sentence, not a parenthesis.
all.fix: Expand the parenthesis once, here: "(80% range 6%-48% — the band the true figure sits in about four times out of five)". Later uses can then stay terse.

all.where: Visual 7 note ("Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta guide to about $717.5 billion of capital spending in 2026") and series sublabel "MSFT + AMZN + GOOGL + META, 2026 guided"
all.why_opaque: "Guide" as an intransitive investor-relations verb is invisible jargon — it looks like ordinary English, so a reader does not even register that they have missed something; they parse it as the companies steering or leading toward a figure. The meaning that matters is that $717.5B is a company forecast, not money spent, which is the difference between T5's supply having arrived and merely being promised. "2026 guided" as a standalone sublabel is worse, with no verb to lean on.
all.fix: Say it plainly in the note: "...have told investors to expect about $717.5 billion of capital spending in 2026", and make the sublabel "2026 company forecasts".

all.where: Visual 8 note ("Anthropic's newer tokenizer counts about 30% more tokens for the same text") and series label "Anthropic tokenizer inflation"
all.why_opaque: Even a reader who has absorbed T6's definition of a token will not know a tokenizer is the chopping rule, or that a lab can change it and thereby change the bill without touching the posted price. "Tokenizer inflation" as a bar label compounds it by borrowing a second economic term for what is really a change in measurement. This is the whole mechanism of the chart: the meter got finer while the rate stayed the same.
all.fix: One clause in the note: "Anthropic's newer tokenizer — the rule that chops text into tokens — counts about 30% more tokens for the same text at an unchanged posted rate."

all.where: Visual 1 series sublabel "the flour: power on a chip someone bought"; Visual 2 title "The ovens: fixed costs are large, and headlines hide them"
all.why_opaque: The analogy is used before it is introduced. Nothing in the standfirst or the six points mentions a bakery, so "the flour:" opens the first chart's key label with a non sequitur, and Visual 2's title reads as a typo. The mapping is genuinely good — oven bought once, flour per loaf — but the reader has to reverse-engineer it from two fragments.
all.fix: Set it up once in T1, in a clause: "Building a model is a fixed cost, like a bakery's oven — you pay it before any sale; each answer is the flour." The two labels then pay off instead of puzzling.

all.where: Visual 2 unit: "USD, millions (log scale)"
all.why_opaque: A reader who does not know the convention will read the bars as if the axis were linear and badly under-feel the gap — the note's own point is that $1.4B is about 250x the $5.6M headline, but on a log axis that bar is only a few times longer. The chart's honesty depends on the reader knowing the axis compresses.
all.fix: Expand in the unit string: "USD, millions (log scale — each step is 10x, not one more)".

all.where: Visual 7 unit "$ billions, 2026 capex (Big-4 hyperscalers)" and series label "Big-4 hyperscaler capex"
all.why_opaque: The note names Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, which tells the reader who but not what the word means or why these four are a category — that they are the firms that own the data centres everyone else rents. "Big-4" also borrows a phrase readers associate with accounting firms.
all.fix: One clause in the note: "Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta — the four firms that own most of the world's rentable computing — have told investors to expect about $717.5 billion..."

all.where: Visual 2 series sublabel: "~50k Hopper GPUs, outside estimate"
all.why_opaque: "Hopper" is an Nvidia chip-generation codename and means nothing without that context; a reader may take it for a vendor, a product, or a metaphor. It is carrying the credibility of the $1.4B estimate — the fleet is specific and datable — and that force is lost.
all.fix: "~50k Nvidia Hopper-generation GPUs, outside estimate".

all.where: Visual 1 note: "Grade C: a triangulation across SemiAnalysis, Martin Alderson and DeepSeek's own disclosure"
all.why_opaque: The first evidence grade a reader meets, with no scale given: is C out of five, out of ten, good or bad? The design spec renders A/B/C grades as chart chrome, so if there is no persistent legend the reader is guessing on the single most important number in the section. "Triangulation" is also being used in its technical sense (an estimate reconciled from partial, non-overlapping sources), not the loose one.
all.fix: Gloss the scale at first use: "Grade C, our weakest tier — no direct disclosure, so this is triangulated from three partial sources: SemiAnalysis, Martin Alderson and DeepSeek's own numbers." (Or ship a fixed A/B/C legend and this drops away.)

all.where: Standfirst ("every answer burns real compute"); T1 ("Anthropic spent an estimated $4.1 billion on research compute in 2025"); Visual 2 series label "Anthropic 2025 research compute"
all.why_opaque: "Compute" as a mass noun is industry usage; in general English it is a verb. "Burns real compute" is roughly inferable from context, but "$4.1 billion on research compute" as a spending category is not — the reader cannot tell whether that is chips, electricity, rent, salaries, or all of it, which matters because the bar is being compared with a $490M training run.
all.fix: Gloss once at the money figure in T1: "...spent an estimated $4.1 billion on research compute — chip time for training and experiments — in 2025."

all.term: compute (as a mass noun priced in dollars)
all.where: Point 2 ("Most of its compute never makes a shipped model"; "OpenAI's 2024 research-and-training compute was about $4.5B"); visual 1 unit "USD millions (final training run compute)" and note; visual 2 unit "USD billions per year (compute only)", labels "OpenAI · R&D + training compute", "Anthropic · inference (serving) compute"; visual 2 note ("the yearly compute bill", "the compute spent on research and training")
all.why_opaque: This is the chapter's load-bearing unit and it is never glossed anywhere in the section (nor in ch.1, which uses it first in its standfirst). To a reader with no AI background "compute" is a verb; used as a countable, purchasable quantity billed in billions of dollars it means chip time bought or rented. Without the gloss the reader cannot tell whether "$4.5B of compute" means chips purchased, cloud hours rented, or the electricity bill — and the whole fixed-vs-variable argument turns on that. Two-syllable common-looking word, so every readability formula waves it through.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in point 2: "Most of its compute (the chip time it buys or rents) never makes a shipped model." Same clause belongs at the ch.1 standfirst if that is the true first use.

all.where: Visual 1, series "xAI Grok 4", sublabel: "2025 · 246M H100-hours"
all.why_opaque: A bare unit presented as if self-evident. H100 is Nvidia's training chip; an H100-hour is one such chip running for one hour. A reader with no background sees a model number fused to a time unit and cannot convert "246M H100-hours" into any picture at all, so the sublabel that is meant to make $490M concrete instead makes it more abstract.
all.fix: Expand the sublabel to one clause: "2025 · 246M H100-hours (one hour of one Nvidia training chip)".

all.where: Visual 1, series "OpenAI GPT-5", sublabel: "2025 · Fermi estimate from FLOP"
all.why_opaque: An unexpanded technical acronym (floating-point operations — the count of arithmetic a training run performs, the standard physical measure of compute). Read cold it looks like the English word "flop", i.e. a failure, which inverts the meaning of the sublabel. Nothing anywhere in the section expands it.
all.fix: "2025 · estimated from FLOP (the count of arithmetic steps the run performed)".

all.where: Visual 5, series "DeepSeek-R1 reasoning add-on", sublabel: "RL phase on top of V3"
all.why_opaque: A bare two-letter acronym, never expanded in this section or in ch.1. Reinforcement learning is the reward-based training step that turned V3 into a reasoning model; without it the reader cannot understand what the $294K bought or why it is an "add-on" rather than a second model. Two characters, so no readability formula can flag it.
all.fix: "a reinforcement-learning step (training by rewarding good answers) on top of V3".

all.where: Visual 1, series "Meta Llama 3.1 405B", sublabel: "2024 · open weights, given away"
all.why_opaque: "Weights" are the trained numbers that *are* the model; "open weights" means the file is public and anyone can download and run it. "Given away" hints that something is free but never says what. The section's own plain_check claims weights is explained the first time it appears — it is not, here or in ch.1 (which uses "open-weight" and "releasing the weights" with no gloss). This is the whole reason a $110M run appears in a chart about what labs spend and never recover.
all.fix: "2024 · open weights (the trained model file is public, free to download and run)".

all.where: Visual 4 unit "USD millions per year (log)" and note "(log axis)"; visual 5 unit "USD millions (log)" and note "(log axis)"; visual 1 note "On a straight linear scale DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2 are near-invisible slivers"
all.why_opaque: A reader who does not know that each step on a log axis multiplies rather than adds will misread the bars: the $6,000M stock-comp bar will look roughly twice the $50M licensing bar rather than 120 times it, which destroys the exact contrast the note asks them to see ("roughly 100x the single training run"). The notes lean on the reader already understanding the device.
all.fix: On first use: "USD millions per year (log axis: each step is 10x, so huge gaps fit in one frame)".

all.where: Visual 1 note ("Whiskers are the calibrated 80% intervals"; "(fx-02, 80% range 2x-3.1x)"); visual 3 note ("38%, 80% range 26-52%"; "the calibrated claim fx-16")
all.why_opaque: The note defines what the whiskers *are* (the intervals) but never what an 80% interval *means*. Lay readers commonly read "80%" as "80% accurate" or "a 20% margin of error". "Calibrated" is a forecasting term of art (the estimator's intervals have been checked against outcomes) that reads here as decoration. Since uncertainty is the honesty device of the entire chart, a misread is expensive.
all.fix: "Whiskers are the calibrated 80% intervals: four times in five we expect the true number to sit inside the whisker."

all.where: Visual 1, GPT-5 sublabel "2025 · Fermi estimate from FLOP"; visual 4 note "a rough Fermi estimate built from vendor revenue, grade C"
all.why_opaque: A named method presented as common knowledge. It means an order-of-magnitude figure built by multiplying out plausible parts rather than measuring. Reads as a proper noun the reader is expected to already recognise, and without it "Fermi estimate" and "our estimate" (grade C) look like two different, unexplained kinds of number.
all.fix: At first use: "a Fermi estimate (the parts multiplied out to get the right order of magnitude)".

all.where: Point 3 ("Research staff, counting their stock grants, take about 38 percent"); point 4 ("OpenAI's stock grants alone ran near $6B a year"); visual 3 label "Research staff (incl. equity)"; visual 4 label "OpenAI stock compensation" with sublabel "2025 · equity alone"
all.why_opaque: Pay in company shares — at firms with no public share price — is finance jargon that a reader with no background will either take as ordinary cash wages or dismiss as not-real money. Either misreading breaks the chapter's biggest single number ($6B/yr, "roughly 100x the single training run"). "incl. equity" in the stack label is more opaque still, since "equity" alone has a completely different everyday meaning (fairness).
all.fix: Gloss at first use in point 3: "counting their stock grants (shares in the company handed out as pay)", then "stock grants" plainly thereafter; change the stack label to "Research staff (incl. stock grants)".

all.term: claim IDs in prose: fx-02, fx-12, fx-13, fx-16 ("the calibrated claim fx-16")
all.where: Visual 1 note ("Epoch AI finds these runs have grown about 2.5x a year since 2016 (fx-02, 80% range 2x-3.1x)"); visual 2 note ("the same two Epoch data-insight posts that fx-12 and fx-13 cite"); visual 3 note ("is the calibrated claim fx-16")
all.why_opaque: Internal reference codes appear in reader-facing note text with no key anywhere in the section. The reader cannot tell whether fx-16 is a source, a footnote, a dataset or a chart series, and "the same two posts that fx-12 and fx-13 cite" asks them to reason about objects they have never been shown. "Calibrated claim" compounds it by making fx-16 sound like a technical object.
all.fix: Name the system once at first use — "(claim fx-02 in our claim ledger, 80% range 2x-3.1x)" — and replace bare IDs in the other two notes with the thing itself ("the two Epoch posts behind these figures").

all.where: Visual 1, series "Google Gemini 1.0 Ultra", sublabel: "2023 · cloud-rental basis"
all.why_opaque: The phrase is doing real comparability work — it flags that this cost was priced as if the chips were rented by the hour rather than owned, which is why it is not strictly like-for-like with the neighbouring bars — but a reader with no background will read it as a source note and skip it. Nothing on the page says the two costing bases differ or by how much.
all.fix: "2023 · costed as rented cloud chips, not owned".

all.where: Visual 3 note: "this split excludes data and licensing, which sit outside Epoch's model"
all.why_opaque: After a section in which "model" always means an AI model (title, every bar label, "one model's development cost" in the very same unit line), "Epoch's model" suddenly means Epoch's cost model. The reader parses it as an AI model Epoch built and stalls.
all.fix: "which sit outside Epoch's cost model".

all.term: frontier (frontier model / frontier lab / US frontier runs)
all.where: Title "What a Frontier Model Costs to Build"; standfirst "the real fixed cost of a frontier lab"; visual 1 note "next to the US frontier runs"; visual 3 note "a frontier model's development cost"
all.why_opaque: Industry shorthand for the handful of most capable models being built at any moment. A curious reader will guess "cutting-edge" and get most of it, but will miss that it denotes a specific small set of labs — which is what makes "several billion dollars a year" a claim about an entire tier rather than about one company.
all.fix: One clause in the standfirst: "a frontier lab (one of the handful building the most capable models)".

all.where: Standfirst ("the real fixed cost of a frontier lab"); point 4 ("People and data are quiet fixed costs too"); visual 4 title and note
all.why_opaque: Defined once in ch.1 point 1 ("Building a model is a fixed cost. You pay it before any sale") and never again, yet this section's own plain_check asserts it is explained here. It is not. Anyone landing on this section directly, or reading the standfirst as a standalone deck, hits the term cold — and it is the section's organising idea.
all.fix: Add the clause back in the standfirst: "the real fixed cost (money spent before a single sale) of a frontier lab".

all.where: Visual 4 (line, "Hold quality fixed and the price falls off a cliff") — both series labels read "GPT-3-grade text (MMLU ~42)", and the note opens "Cheapest model clearing GPT-3-grade quality (MMLU ~42)"
all.why_opaque: A bare four-letter acronym with no expansion anywhere in chapters 1-3 or the page footer. It is also load-bearing rather than decorative: the entire visual rests on "hold quality fixed", and MMLU ~42 IS the definition of fixed quality. A reader who cannot decode it cannot tell whether the thousand-fold price fall is a like-for-like comparison or a bait-and-switch, which is exactly the objection the chart exists to answer.
all.fix: Gloss once at first use in the note: "Cheapest model clearing GPT-3-grade quality (MMLU ~42, the standard multi-subject exam score used to rank models)". Series labels can then stay as they are.

all.where: Visual 2 (range) — series label "Marginal serving cost ÷ API list price", and note "SemiAnalysis works back from a 75% API gross margin, implying cost is 25% of list"
all.why_opaque: Never expanded or glossed anywhere on the page. It also carries a distinction the reader needs and is never told: every price in this chapter is the pay-per-token price developers are charged, not the $20-a-month subscription a reader personally pays. Without that, a reader silently maps "$30 per million output tokens" onto the wrong product. The chapter's own plain_check claims "rate card" was used instead of "API list price" — but the chart label still says API list price, so the fix was applied to the prose and not to the chart furniture.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in the visual 2 note: "a 75% margin on API sales — the pay-per-token channel developers buy through, not the monthly consumer subscription", and simplify the series label to "Marginal serving cost ÷ list price".

all.where: Visual 1 (bars_ci) — series sublabel for the $3 bar: "napkin model, frontier MoE on rented H100s"
all.why_opaque: An unexpanded acronym (mixture-of-experts) sitting in the sublabel the reader looks at while reading the single most important cost estimate in the chapter. It appears nowhere else in the section, so there is no context to decode it from, and "napkin model" beside it compounds the problem. The reader's most likely response is to distrust the $3 estimate because its provenance line is unreadable.
all.fix: Either gloss it in one clause — "napkin model, frontier mixture-of-experts model (only part of it runs per answer) on rented H100s" — or, since MoE carries no argumentative weight anywhere in this section, drop the acronym: "back-of-envelope model, top-tier model on rented H100 chips". No idea is lost either way.

all.why_opaque: The abbreviation is never expanded at or before first use. The page footer says "Shaded bands are 80% confidence intervals" but that sits at the very end of the page and never ties the letters C-I to those words. Worse, chapter 3 is inconsistent with itself and with the rest of the page: the same quantity is called "band" (v1, v2, v7, v9), "80% range" (chapters 1 and 2), "80% intervals" (chapter 2), "whiskers" (v1, v10) and "80% CI" here. A reader meeting five names for one thing concludes they are five different things.
all.fix: Use the wording chapters 1 and 2 already use — "80% range 8-200" — or expand once at first use in v4: "80% confidence interval (the band the true number sits in four times out of five) 8-200". Then pick one name and hold it for the whole chapter.

all.where: Point 5 ("Whole-company gross margin at OpenAI is nearer 42%"); visual 9 unit ("% gross margin"), title ("Fat margin on the token, thin margin on the firm") and note ("whole-company adjusted gross margin for FY2025"); visual 2 note ("works back from a 75% API gross margin")
all.why_opaque: Defined only implicitly and two chapters earlier — chapter 1's visual 3 pairs the title "Of every $100 charged, how much is left after cost?" with the unit "% gross margin", and chapter 1's point 1 says "keeps only about 43 cents of each sales dollar". A reader has to notice that pairing and carry it across two chapters. Chapter 3 then leans on the term far harder than chapter 1 did, and the visual 2 sentence "works back from a 75% API gross margin, implying cost is 25% of list" additionally requires the reader to already know margin and cost-share are complements. Point 5 also uses "margin" in three senses within six sentences (per-token margin, fleet margin, whole-company gross margin), and visual 3's note adds a fourth ("the chip maker takes a margin").
all.fix: Re-gloss cheaply at first use in point 5: "Whole-company gross margin at OpenAI — what is left of each sales dollar after the direct cost of delivering it — is nearer 42%." One clause, no idea removed.

all.where: Visual 7 (slope) — unit "$ per GPU-hour"; note "$0.06-0.17/GPU-hour for power against a ~$2.35/hr rental"
all.why_opaque: The chapter's prose deliberately and consistently says "chip" ("burns time on a real chip", "one H100 chip", "Rent on an H100 chip rose too", "The cost is the chip") — and then the unit label, one of the most-read strings on any chart, switches to GPU without warning. GPU is never expanded anywhere on the page. The reader must silently infer both that GPU means the chip they were just told about and that a GPU-hour is one chip running for one hour, which is the whole basis of the rental price and of the electricity share computed in the same note.
all.fix: Make the unit match the prose: "$ per chip-hour (one H100 running for one hour)". If GPU must stay for accuracy, gloss it once in the note: "per GPU-hour — the rent on one chip for one hour".

all.where: Visual 10 (bars_ci) — series sublabel: "output tokens (input $0.28, cache-hit $0.028)"
all.why_opaque: Pure infrastructure jargon with no gloss anywhere on the page and no surrounding context to decode from. A reader with no technical background cannot guess that it means text the model has already been sent and can bill at a tenth of the rate. It also actively confuses the visual's point: a reader who half-guesses may think the real Chinese price is $0.028, undercutting the note's careful argument that this is not a Chinese cost edge.
all.fix: Replace the term with its meaning in the sublabel: "output tokens (input $0.28; text already sent before, $0.028)". If the term is wanted, "cache-hit input (text the model has seen before) $0.028".

all.term: input vs output tokens / "per M in/out"
all.where: Point 2 ("lists at $5 in and $30 out per million tokens"); point 4 ("The flagship input price"); visual 5 sublabels ("Jun 2025 — $10/$40 to $2/$8 per M in/out"; "Nov 2025 — $15/$75 to $5/$25 per M in/out"); visual 1 note ("Headline values for px-12 and px-13 are the input prices")
all.why_opaque: The page tells the reader what a token is (chapter 1, point 5) but never once says that models charge two different prices — one for the text you send, one for the text they write back — or why. From point 2 onward the reader is handed paired numbers with no explanation, and the sublabel notation "$10/$40 to $2/$8 per M in/out" compresses four prices, an abbreviation for million, and the undefined in/out split into eleven characters. It also matters for the argument: visual 6's note turns on output prices having fallen far less than input prices, which is unreadable if the distinction was never established.
all.fix: Establish it once in point 2: "OpenAI's top tier lists at $5 for the text you send in and $30 for the text it writes back, per million tokens." Then unpack the sublabel notation: "Jun 2025 — $10/$40 down to $2/$8 per million tokens, in / out".

all.where: Visual 1 (bars_ci) — series sublabel for the $0.26 bar: "measured benchmark, production-style batching"
all.why_opaque: Undefined anywhere on the page, and it is doing real evidentiary work rather than decorating: the $0.26 figure — the lowest cost bar, and the one that most strengthens the price-umbrella argument — is only achievable because many requests are answered together on one chip. A reader who cannot decode the caveat cannot judge whether that number is realistic or a lab-bench artefact, which is precisely what the sublabel was written to tell them.
all.fix: Say it in plain words in the sublabel: "measured benchmark, many requests answered at once as in production".

all.where: Visual 9 (bars_ci) — final sentence of the note: "Training is not in this line at all — it books as research."
all.why_opaque: An accounting idiom compressed into four words. "Books as" (is recorded in the accounts as) and "this line" (this line item) are both trade usage, and the sentence carries a genuinely important idea — that the enormous training bill from chapter 2 is excluded from these margin figures by an accounting convention, not because it does not exist. A reader who cannot parse it loses the single most important caveat on the 72% and 42% numbers.
all.fix: Unpack in one clause: "Training is not counted in these margins at all — it is booked as research spending, not as a cost of serving."

all.where: Visual 10 title ("Where price does track cost: open weights") and note ("Anyone can host a model whose weights are public"); point 5 ("The cheapest host of one open model"); visual 10 sublabel ("open-weight market")
all.why_opaque: The visual 10 note gives a good functional definition of what open weights let you do, but it arrives after the title has already used the term, after point 5 has used "open model", and after chapters 1 and 2 used "open weights" and "before releasing the weights" with no gloss. And "weights" itself — the trained numbers that constitute the model — is never explained anywhere on the page, so the note's definition only works for a reader who already had it.
all.fix: Add three words to the existing note sentence: "Anyone can host a model whose weights — the trained numbers that are the model — are published, so hosts compete on cost alone."

all.where: Visual 7 (slope) — both series labels: "H100 SXM, 1-year contract rental"
all.why_opaque: A chip form-factor designation with no expansion, no context and no argumentative weight in this section. It reads as an unexplained code in the most prominent text on the chart, and its only effect on a lay reader is to signal that this chart is not written for them.
all.fix: Drop it: "H100, one-year contract rental". If the precision is needed for sourcing, move it to the note rather than the series label.

all.where: Visual 4 (line) — end of note: "the path between them is not in the data layer and is not invented here"
all.why_opaque: Internal project vocabulary leaking into reader-facing copy. "Data layer" refers to this project's structured claims file, a thing the reader has never been told exists. The sentence is making a genuinely admirable point about not interpolating uncertified data, and that point simply does not land.
all.fix: Use reader-facing words: "the path between them is not in the certified data, and is not invented here".

all.where: Visual 9 series label ("Anthropic — inference infrastructure") and note ("Anthropic's inference-infrastructure margin"; "OpenAI's Azure inference spend"); visual 5 note quote ("We optimized our inference stack")
all.why_opaque: The chapter's stated policy is to say "serving" instead of "inference", and the prose honours it — but the word survives in a chart series label and two notes, so the reader is asked to equate two words without help. The only gloss on the page is a parenthetical in chapter 2's chart labels, "inference (serving) compute", which is remote and easy to miss. The reader is then asked to accept that "inference infrastructure" (72%) and "whole company" (42%) are two different accounting scopes of the same business — an argument that fails if the first phrase is opaque.
all.fix: Either rename the series label "Anthropic — serving infrastructure" to match the prose, or reuse chapter 2's gloss on first appearance: "inference (serving) infrastructure".

all.where: Visual 9 (bars_ci) — note: "and idle time — effective fleet utilization is put near 40%, band 25-65%"
all.why_opaque: "Idle time" immediately before it does most of the work, so this is a near miss rather than a miss. But "utilization" is undefined and the direction is ambiguous to a lay reader: 40% utilization could plausibly be read as 40% idle rather than 40% busy, which flips the sign of the point being made. "Fleet" as a term for a set of chips is also introduced without comment (point 5 uses "serving fleet").
all.fix: State the number in the direction the reader needs: "and idle time — the chip fleet is only about 40% busy, band 25-65%".

all.where: Visual 10 — series sublabel "open-weight market, blended in/out, Jun 2026", and note "mc-14 is a blended input/output price"
all.why_opaque: Trade shorthand for a weighted average of the input and output prices. The note's unit caveat gets close by contrasting it with "output-only", but the term first appears in a sublabel, and repeating the word inside its own explanation ("a blended input/output price") does not define it. It matters because this bar is compared against two output-only bars, which is the caveat the note is trying to raise.
all.fix: Say what it is in the sublabel: "open-weight market, input and output averaged, Jun 2026", and in the note: "mc-14 averages the input and output price together, the other two are output-only".

all.where: Visual 3 (bars_ci) title: "The life call: what firms book against what Epoch measures"; then every sublabel ("booked, servers and network gear", "booked, GPUs and technology equipment", "booked — the only firm that SHORTENED"); note: "Every buyer books five to six years" and "The disclosed book lives are exact"; also Visual 4 sublabel "short-lived: booked at 5–6 years"
all.why_opaque: One syllable, everyday word, invisible to every readability formula — and it carries the entire load-bearing idea of the chart. To a reader with no finance background "book" means reserve a table or a physical object; the accounting sense (the figure a firm records in its own accounts, as opposed to what is physically true) is never stated. Without it the chart's whole point — that the booked life is a claim and Epoch's 3.9 years is a measurement — collapses into two numbers that just differ. The section leans on this contrast four separate times.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in the Visual 3 title or the first line of its note: "Useful life is the number of years a firm books — records in its own accounts — that a chip will keep earning." Every later "booked" then reads correctly with no further change.

all.where: Visual 4 (stack) unit label: "% of hyperscaler capital spending"
all.why_opaque: Pure industry jargon with no everyday meaning to fall back on, sitting in a unit label where there is no surrounding sentence to infer from. It is undefined anywhere on the page — Ch.1's unit label "(Big-4 hyperscalers)" uses it bare as well, so a reader arriving at Ch.4 has met the word twice and been told nothing. The section otherwise says "four US giants" and "big cloud firms" in plain English, so this is also an unforced inconsistency.
all.fix: Change the unit to "% of capital spending by the big cloud firms", or keep the term with a clause in the note's first sentence: "Of every dollar the hyperscalers — the giant cloud firms — lay out, about 58 cents buys servers and chips."

all.where: Point 5: "CoreWeave counters that lapsed chips re-signed at about 95% of the old price."
all.why_opaque: Four common words that encode a contract-renewal mechanic. The natural reading is that the chips themselves lapsed (expired? failed?) and were somehow re-signed. What is actually meant — rental contracts that reached their end date were renewed at roughly the old rate — is nowhere on the page, and this is the single sentence rebutting Burry's $176bn charge, so a reader who misreads it loses the counter-argument entirely.
all.fix: "CoreWeave counters that chips whose rental contracts ran out were re-let at about 95% of the old price." Same length, same idea, no new syllables.

all.where: Visual 1 series sublabels: "guided, 2026", "guided $195–205B, raised 22 Jul 2026", "guided, calendar 2026", "guided $125–145B, midpoint", "guided $30–35B, midpoint"; Visual 1 note: "The parts here are guidance midpoints"; Visual 2 note: "2026 guidance on the right" and "its 2026 guide is about $190 billion"; Visual 2 sublabels "2026 guided"
all.why_opaque: Looks like plain English and reads as if someone advised the firm, or as an editorial estimate. It actually means a specific, consequential thing: the company's own public forecast of its future spending — a promise it made, not an outside guess. That distinction is the whole reason the chart can be graded A and still be uncertain, and the whole meaning of Point 3's "Those are plans, not signed cash." It appears roughly ten times across two charts and is never once defined.
all.fix: Gloss at first note use in Visual 1: "The parts here are guidance midpoints — the middle of each firm's own public spending forecast — so they add to roughly $725B." The sublabels then decode on their own.

all.where: Visual 1 note: "(cx-11, grade B, 80% range $655–790B)" and "(cx-12, grade B, range $850B–$1.28T)"; recurs in Visual 4 and Visual 5 notes; page footer says only "Shaded bands are 80% confidence intervals"
all.why_opaque: The footer restates the jargon rather than defining it, and it sits at the very bottom of the page — long after first use. "80% range" is short and numeric so it sails through every formula, but a reader with no statistics background cannot tell whether the 80% refers to the number, the sources, or the odds. Since the honesty of this whole section rests on its intervals (Visual 5's entire message is "certain in direction, vague in size"), the reader needs to know what the band asserts.
all.fix: One clause at the first appearance: "80% range $655–790B — meaning we would put four-in-five odds on the true figure landing inside that band."

all.term: grade A / grade B (and the bare claim ids, e.g. cx-11)
all.where: Visual 1 note: "(cx-11, grade B, 80% range $655–790B)", "(cx-12, grade B...)"; Visual 4 note "(cx-17, grade B)"; Visual 5 note "(dp-13, grade B)", "(dp-14, grade B)"; grade letters also render on the chart marks and in the sources list
all.why_opaque: The scheme IS defined — "Grades: A filed/official · B credible reporting · C our own triangulation" — but only in the page footer, i.e. after every single use, and Ch.4 is the fourth chapter a reader meets grades in. Inside the note, "grade B" reads as a school mark, implying the number is mediocre rather than sourced-to-reporting-not-a-filing. The parenthetical id "cx-11" compounds it: an unexplained code in the middle of a prose sentence.
all.fix: Expand the first grade mention in the section: "(claim cx-11, grade B — credible reporting rather than a company filing, 80% range $655–790B)". Later ones can stay bare.

all.where: Visual 2 (slope) note: "Microsoft is left off because there is no clean 2025 actual in the claims layer; its 2026 guide is about $190 billion (cx-01)."
all.why_opaque: Internal build-architecture vocabulary that has leaked into reader-facing copy. It refers to this project's sourced claim database, but nothing on the page tells the reader such a thing exists or that it is the arbiter of what gets charted. As written it sounds like a technical stratum of the data centre business, which is exactly the wrong inference in a chapter about capex.
all.fix: "Microsoft is left off because we have no cleanly sourced 2025 actual for it; its 2026 guide is about $190 billion."

all.where: Point 2: "One warning: dollars are not compute."; Point 3: "OpenAI has announced roughly $1.25 trillion of compute deals"; Visual 1 note: "One caveat: dollars are not compute."
all.why_opaque: Compute is normally a verb. Used as an uncountable noun meaning the quantity of raw processing power, it is AI-industry shorthand a general reader has to guess at. Point 2's follow-on ("the spend curve is steeper than the capacity curve") gestures at the meaning but never names it, and "capacity curve" is itself unexplained. The distinction carries a genuinely important caveat — that the spending chart overstates the capacity being built — so a fuzzy read costs the reader real information.
all.fix: Name it once in Point 2: "One warning: dollars are not compute — the raw computing power the money actually buys." The Visual 1 note echo then works unaided.

all.where: Visual 3 (bars_ci) note: "The disclosed book lives are exact, so they carry no whisker; only the Epoch estimate does."
all.why_opaque: Chart-craft vocabulary borrowed from box plots. To a reader with no background it is either an animal hair or a near-miss. The sentence is doing careful, honest work — telling the reader why one bar has a range mark and the others do not — and that work is lost if the noun is unreadable. This is the same failure class as "rate card": two syllables, common word, zero comprehension.
all.fix: "...so they carry no whisker — the thin line that shows a range — while the Epoch estimate does."

all.where: Point 5: "Epoch AI measures about 3.9 years at the frontier, then a fading tail."; Visual 3 series label "Epoch AI: measured frontier life" and sublabel "release to last frontier model"
all.why_opaque: Defined, but too late. Visual 3's note does gloss it well ("the frontier window — how long a chip design stays in use for training the best models"), yet points render above all visuals, so first use is Point 5 with no gloss, and the series label sits above the note too. A reader meets "at the frontier" cold and will read it geographically or as vague boosterism, which makes the load-bearing comparison — 3.9 measured years versus 5–6 booked years — look like a straight contradiction rather than two different spans.
all.fix: Move the clause up to Point 5: "Epoch AI measures about 3.9 years at the frontier — the span a chip design stays in use training the best models — then a fading tail."

all.where: Visual 5 unit: "% fall in rental price per chip-hour, 2023/24 peak to early 2026"; note: "Big cloud firms charge far more per chip-hour than small renters"; sublabel: "peak to trough, per chip-hour"
all.why_opaque: A compound unit invented by the industry. It is guessable, but the guess is doing real work here: the whole payback argument depends on the reader understanding that this is a rental meter running by the hour, not a price per chip. Ch.3 uses "$ per GPU-hour" for the same idea, so the reader also has to reconcile two different unit names for one thing.
all.fix: Gloss once in the Visual 5 note: "Big cloud firms charge far more per chip-hour — one chip rented for one hour — than small renters."

all.where: Visual 3 series sublabel: "booked, GPUs and technology equipment (from 5yr in 2023)"
all.why_opaque: An unexpanded acronym appearing exactly once, in a chart label, in a section that otherwise says "chips" throughout. A reader who has followed five points about chips now has to work out whether GPUs are the same asset or a different one — and since the sublabel is quoting CoreWeave's disclosure category, getting that wrong makes the bar look non-comparable to the others.
all.fix: "booked, GPUs (the AI chips) and technology equipment (from 5yr in 2023)".

all.where: Point 5: "Rental prices for H100 chips have fallen roughly 60%"; Visual 5 title: "The clue in prices: H100 rental rates are down about 60%"
all.why_opaque: The surrounding words do tell the reader it is a chip, so this is only partly opaque. What is missing is why this particular chip's price is evidence about the whole wave — that the H100 is Nvidia's workhorse AI chip and its rental rate is the industry's benchmark price. Without that, the reader cannot tell whether a 60% fall in one product is a clue or a footnote.
all.fix: "Rental prices for H100 chips, Nvidia's workhorse AI chip, have fallen roughly 60%..."

all.where: Point 5: "Epoch AI measures about 3.9 years at the frontier"; Visual 3 series label "Epoch AI: measured frontier life" and title "...what firms book against what Epoch measures"
all.why_opaque: Not a term but an unidentified authority carrying the section's pivotal number. The reader is asked to weigh 3.9 years against the filed policies of Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon without being told who Epoch AI is or why their measurement counts. The section glosses its other outsiders ("The investor Michael Burry", "The chip renter CoreWeave"), so this is an inconsistency as much as an omission.
all.fix: "Epoch AI, a research group that tracks AI hardware, measures about 3.9 years at the frontier."

all.term: bars_ci / точные (stray strings in the rendered rationale)
all.where: Visual 3 viz_rationale, which build_p1.py renders to the reader inside the collapsible "sources" block: "bars_ci rather than plain bars because exactly one value here is an estimate... while the filed policies are точные disclosures."
all.why_opaque: Two separate leaks in one reader-visible sentence. "bars_ci" is the internal chart-type key from the spec, meaningless to a reader. "точные" is a Russian word ("exact") left in the English copy — almost certainly an editing accident. Neither is jargon the reader can decode, and neither is reachable by any readability gate, since the rationale is not part of the points' budget.
all.fix: Rewrite as: "A ranged bar rather than a plain one, because exactly one value here is an estimate: Epoch's 3.9 years needs its range visible, while the filed policies are exact disclosures."

all.where: point 5, final sentence: "OpenAI raised near $852 billion and Anthropic near $965 billion."
all.why_opaque: The reader takes "raised" in its plain sense — cash the company collected — and that reading is wrong by an order of magnitude. Both underlying claims are post-money VALUATIONS (rv-09 unit: "USD billions (post-money valuation)", value 852; rv-15 same, value 965). OpenAI raised $122B at an $852B valuation; Anthropic raised $65B at a $965B valuation. The section then prints its own contradiction two charts away, in the source line "Anthropic raises $65B in Series H funding at $965B post-money valuation" — so the attentive reader sees $965B raised in the text and $65B raised in the citation and cannot reconcile them. "Raised" is one common two-syllable word, so no readability formula can see this.
all.fix: "Backers are betting the gap holds: they now value OpenAI near $852 billion and Anthropic near $965 billion — the price put on the whole firm, not cash in the bank."

all.term: at the operating line / operating loss / operating profit
all.where: point 4, first sentence ("lost about $21 billion at the operating line"); visual 3 note ("$20.92B operating loss", "first quarterly operating profit"); series label "OpenAI · operating loss"; sublabel "Q2 2026 guided operating profit"
all.why_opaque: First use anywhere on the page is here — chapters 1-4 never use it. "Operating" is the accountant's fence between running the business and one-off items, and the whole of point 4 plus the whole diverging chart hang on it. The gap is immediately visible to the reader and unbridgeable: the chart shows -$20.92B while the sublabel beside it says "net loss $38.5B". With no definition, the reader cannot tell whether OpenAI lost $21B or $38.5B, or why the page picked the smaller one. "At the operating line" is also a metaphor (a row in the accounts) the reader has no anchor for.
all.fix: point 4: "OpenAI lost about $21 billion at the operating line in 2025 — the loss on running the business, before one-off items — even as revenue tripled."

all.where: point 4 ("it was fundraise guidance, not an audited result"); visual 2 note ("Anthropic's 40% is 2025 guidance") and sublabel ("FY2025 guidance"); visual 3 note ("Anthropic guides to ~$3B burn") and sublabels ("guides to ~$3B in 2026", "guided operating profit")
all.why_opaque: Everyday "guidance" means advice or direction. The finance sense — a forecast the company itself publishes to investors, unaudited and self-serving — is exactly the load-bearing caveat of point 4 and of two chart notes. A lay reader parses "fundraise guidance" as "guidelines for fundraising" and the warning evaporates. Six occurrences in this section, all undefined; the contrast "not an audited result" hints at unreliability but never says what the word means.
all.fix: point 4: "it was fundraise guidance — a number the company itself projected for investors — not an audited result"

all.where: visual 3 ("The fixed side"), opening sentence of the note
all.why_opaque: "Signed" here is chart-convention jargon meaning "carries a plus or minus sign". The reader has just read, in point 5, "OpenAI has signed about $1.4 trillion of data-centre commitments" — so the overwhelmingly likely reading is a contract that was signed, and "signed around zero" then reads as nonsense. Two one-syllable words: structurally invisible to Flesch-Kincaid, Fog and SMOG.
all.fix: Replace with "Bars run above and below zero." — the next sentence ("Below the line is money going out") already carries the meaning the jargon was reaching for.

all.where: point 2, first three words
all.why_opaque: Income-statement jargon: revenue is the top row of the accounts. Sole use on the whole page, and it opens the point cold, so the reader hits it with no context and no gloss. It also sits in a section that separately asks the reader to hold "the fixed side", "the operating line" and "the research line" — four different rows of an accounts document, none named as such.
all.fix: "The top line — revenue, before any cost is taken out — is growing faster than almost anything on record, and it sits in two firms."

all.where: visual 3, OpenAI sublabel: "FY2025; net loss $38.5B including ~$30B one-time conversion charges"
all.why_opaque: "Conversion" refers to OpenAI's restructuring from nonprofit to for-profit; nothing anywhere on the page says so, and "charge" in the accounting sense (a cost booked without cash leaving) is a second undefined term stacked on the first. The sublabel also introduces a second loss figure nearly double the charted one ($38.5B vs $20.92B) with no bridge, so its net effect on an untrained reader is to make the chart look wrong.
all.fix: "FY2025; net loss $38.5B, including ~$30B of one-off charges from OpenAI's switch to a for-profit structure"

all.term: cost of revenue (and "a derivation, not a disclosure")
all.where: visual 2 note: "OpenAI's 42.6% is a derivation, not a disclosure: $13.07B of revenue less $7.5B of cost of revenue"; also the source line "(cost of revenue $7.5B)"
all.why_opaque: Reads to a lay ear as "the cost of having revenue", which is circular. It is in fact the accounts line for direct serving cost — the same thing point 3 defined in plain words as "the direct cost of serving it" — but nothing tells the reader the two phrases are the same quantity, so the note's arithmetic looks like it appeared from nowhere. "Disclosure" carries a parallel technical sense (a figure the company itself published) that the reader will not have.
all.fix: "OpenAI's 42.6% is a figure we worked out, not one the company published: $13.07B of revenue less $7.5B of cost of revenue — that same direct serving cost."

all.where: visual 2 note: "A large slice of serving compute appears to sit in the research line instead, so the true serving margin is lower."
all.why_opaque: "Line" again means a row in a company's accounts, never explained. This sentence carries the note's single most important caveat — that the charted 42.6% overstates the truth — and it is unreadable without knowing that companies file costs into named rows and can put a cost in one row rather than another.
all.fix: "appears to sit in the research line — the research-and-development row of the accounts — instead"

all.where: point 5 ("plans its first positive cash flow in 2030"); visual 3 series label "Anthropic · cash burn" and note "OpenAI plans to burn $25B in 2026 alone"
all.why_opaque: This is the fourth distinct money-out measure the section uses — after operating loss, cash burn and operating profit — and none of the four is distinguished from the others. The reader most naturally hears "first positive cash flow in 2030" as "first profit in 2030", which flatly contradicts the Anthropic "first quarterly operating profit" the section already reported for Q2 2026, and leaves them unable to tell why OpenAI's $21B loss and its $25B burn are different numbers.
all.fix: point 5: "plans its first year of positive cash flow — more cash coming in than going out — in 2030"

all.where: visual 2 OpenAI sublabel: "API-only adjusted margin ~33% in 2025, ~39% by Q1 2026"; visual 4 xAI sublabel: "SuperGrok, API and enterprise"
all.why_opaque: An undefined acronym in reader-facing text — notable because the section's own plain_check asserts "No undefined acronyms", having checked only the points and not the sublabels. "Adjusted" stacks a second undefined finance term on top of it. The sublabel is doing real work (it quietly concedes the true serving margin is nearer 33% than the charted 42.6%), so the reader who bounces off "API-only adjusted" loses the correction.
all.fix: "API sales only — model access bought by other companies' software — ~33% in 2025, ~39% by Q1 2026"

all.where: visual 4 note, final clause: "they sell picks and shovels, a different and larger pool"
all.why_opaque: A gold-rush idiom (sell tools to the miners, not gold) doing the entire explanatory work of the note's closing point — why Microsoft's $37B and Google Cloud's $24.8B are excluded from a chart about model revenue. A reader who does not already carry the idiom gets no reason at all for the exclusion.
all.fix: "they sell picks and shovels — the compute the labs rent, not the models — a different and larger pool"

all.where: visual 1 sublabels ("FY2025, audited accounts leaked June 2026"; "FY2025, reported by The Information") and note; visual 2 sublabels; visual 3 sublabels; visual 4 note
all.why_opaque: Eight appearances of an abbreviation that is never spelled out. It matters more than usual here because the section's entire argument is a like-for-like timing comparison (run-rate vs recognized, "each pair here is contemporaneous"), and the same page elsewhere shows a fiscal year that is not a calendar year (ch4: "actual, fiscal year to May 2026") — so the reader cannot safely assume FY2025 means 2025.
all.fix: Spell it out once at first use: "financial year 2025 (FY2025), audited accounts leaked June 2026"

all.where: eyebrow "the money · run-rate vs real"; standfirst "the headline run-rates run about double what an auditor will sign"
all.why_opaque: Borderline, and close to handled — point 1 defines it cleanly one sentence later. But the eyebrow is the literal first string the reader sees in the section and it is bare jargon with no gloss, and the standfirst then leans on it again. The standfirst's "run about double what an auditor will sign" tells the reader the number is inflated but never what a run-rate is.
all.fix: standfirst: "the headline run-rates — one strong month multiplied by twelve — run about double what an auditor will sign"

all.where: Visual 4 ("The 2024 cuts were strategy. The 2025 cut was cost.") — series sublabel "sparse attention; tracked a real cost drop", and the note "It shipped with a leaner attention design, so the price followed a real drop in cost." Point 4 gestures at it as "a leaner design".
all.why_opaque: "Attention" in the machine-learning sense appears nowhere else on the whole page and is never explained; "sparse attention" is the only occurrence of the word "sparse" in the entire spec file. It is short, low-syllable, and invisible to the readability gate, but a reader with no AI background cannot recover any meaning from it — "attention" reads as a human faculty, not a part of a model. This matters because the term is the load-bearing evidence for the chapter's key contrast: the 2024 cut was strategy, the 2025 cut was real cost. The reader is asked to accept that an engineering change genuinely lowered cost, and the only word offered as the reason is one they cannot parse.
all.fix: Add a one-clause gloss in the note: "It shipped with a leaner attention design (each new word looks at fewer of the earlier ones), so the price followed a real drop in cost." Sublabel becomes "sparse attention: reads less of the text per step".

all.where: Visual 5 note: "The band shown is the 80 percent interval, 530 to 560 percent." Visual 6 note: "The whisker is the 80 percent range, 250,000 to 1.5 million. That is a six-fold spread..."
all.why_opaque: This is confidence-interval vocabulary wearing plain clothes — five common words that sail through Flesch-Kincaid while conveying nothing. Nowhere on the page is it put into plain terms. Chapter 2's note says "Whiskers are the calibrated 80% intervals", which defines jargon with jargon, and the page footer's "Shaded bands are 80% confidence intervals" is both more jargon and physically after chapter 6. "Whisker" is chart-craft vocabulary for the thin line on the bar and is never identified as such. The cost is highest in visual 6, whose entire title ("The fallback chip supply nobody can size") and argument is that the uncertainty IS the finding — a reader who does not know what an 80 percent range means cannot get the point at all.
all.fix: On first use in the chapter, one clause: "The whisker — the thin line on the bar — is the 80 percent range, 250,000 to 1.5 million, meaning four times in five the true number should land inside it."

all.where: Visual 6 note: "Nvidia took a $4.5B charge in 2025 on China chips it could no longer sell (ce-13, grade A)".
all.why_opaque: Not merely opaque — actively misleading. "Charge" in the accounting sense means a write-off booked against profit, i.e. money lost. But chapter 6 itself uses "charge" three times in the ordinary sense of billing a customer, twice within a few hundred words: "it charged fifteen dollars per million output tokens", "That is what a top US model charges", "you only charge by the hour when your machines are full". A reader with no finance background will carry the everyday sense forward and read "took a $4.5B charge" as Nvidia collecting $4.5B — the exact inverse of the intended meaning, and it inverts the sentence's role as evidence of how badly the export controls bit.
all.fix: Drop the term rather than gloss it, since a plain verb exists: "Nvidia wrote off $4.5B in 2025 on China chips it could no longer sell".

all.where: Visual 3 ("Who eats the fixed cost") — series label "Alibaba AI revenue, guided", sublabel "money back, RMB 30B a year by end-2026".
all.why_opaque: "Guided" here is finance shorthand for company guidance: management's own published forecast, not a result. Stranded as a one-word participle after a comma it is unresolvable to a lay reader, who will read it as "steered" or "approximate". The consequence is structural: this is one of only two "money back" bars carrying the chapter's central asymmetry, and it is not money that has come back at all — it is a company promise about a future year, sitting on the same log axis as audited losses and closed funding rounds. Chapter 5 hints at the distinction ("it was fundraise guidance, not an audited result") but never defines the word, and the hint is a chapter away.
all.fix: Make the label self-explaining: "Alibaba AI revenue, company forecast", with the sublabel "money back, the company's own target of RMB 30B a year by end-2026".

all.where: Point 5: "At list price, serving would have earned far more than the chips cost." Also visual 1 note ("Everything else is a list price"), visual 4 unit ("percent cut off list price"), visual 5 note ("billing every token at R1 list price"), visual 1 sublabel ("US, closed weights, list price").
all.why_opaque: Two ordinary words that any readability formula waves through, and the reader will simply take them to mean "the price". The thing they will miss is the only thing that matters here: a list price is the advertised sticker rate, and most traffic never paid it. That gap is precisely why DeepSeek's 545 percent is labelled "theoretical" and why the company itself said real revenue was far lower. Point 5 makes the claim with no repair; the repair arrives later, inside visual 5's note, which many readers reach after they have already banked "they made five times their costs" as a fact.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in point 5: "At its advertised price, which most users never actually paid, serving would have earned far more than the chips cost."

all.where: Point 3: "So who pays for training? A quant hedge fund."
all.why_opaque: "Quant" appears exactly once on the entire page and is never explained. The sentence is four words long, so it passes every syllable and length test, yet two of those words are finance jargon carrying the answer to the question the chapter's title poses. "Hedge fund" is half-familiar to a general reader; "quant" is not, and it is doing real work — it is because High-Flyer traded by computer that it already owned a large chip fleet and the trading profits to fund one, which is the whole reason a hedge fund is a plausible answer to "who pays for training".
all.fix: One clause: "A quant hedge fund, which trades by computer."

all.where: Visual 2 note: "It is 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours priced at $2 an hour" and "The fleet behind it, roughly 50,000 Hopper chips, is about 250 times larger." Visual 2 sublabel: "about 50,000 Hopper GPUs, estimated".
all.why_opaque: "GPU-hour" is used as a unit on this page (chapter 3) but never defined anywhere, and "GPU" itself is never spelled out. "H800" and "Hopper" are Nvidia product and generation names that read to an outsider as meaningless codes — and worse, the same paragraph switches between "H800", "Hopper chips" and "Hopper GPUs" without signalling these are all the same kind of object. The note's job is to let the reader watch $5.576M get built from a rate and a quantity, which is the entire honesty of the chart; that fails if the quantity is unreadable.
all.fix: Define the unit once and drop the model code: "It is 2.788 million GPU-hours — one chip running for one hour — at $2 each", and "roughly 50,000 Nvidia Hopper chips".

all.where: Visual 5 note, final sentence: "Most of the US-China price gap is a scarcity premium collected on the American side."
all.why_opaque: "Premium" in the pricing sense — an amount charged above cost — is never defined, and the word's dominant everyday meaning is quality (premium product, premium seat). A reader who takes that sense inverts the chapter's conclusion from "Americans can charge more because chips are scarce" into "American models are better, so they cost more", which is the exact reading the chapter spends five points dismantling. This sentence is the chapter's verdict, so the misread is expensive. Chapter 3's "pricing power here is scarcity, not greed" is helpful but sits three chapters back and uses different words.
all.fix: One clause: "a scarcity premium — extra charged simply because chips are hard to get — collected on the American side".

all.where: Visual 1 note: "Matched-quality US-to-China ratio is about 10x, but the honest range is 4x to 40x (ce-17, grade C), because matched quality is a judgment call." Related sublabel: "China, open weights, matched to Sonnet 4.6".
all.why_opaque: A four-word noun pile built from a term of art. "Matched quality" means models judged to be about equally capable, and the ratio is of prices — but neither the comparison nor its direction is stated, so the reader must reverse-engineer that the claim is "for models of similar ability, the US price is roughly ten times the Chinese one". The trailing clause explains why the number is uncertain without ever saying what the number is.
all.fix: Say it as a sentence: "Compare models of similar ability and the US price is about 10x the Chinese one, though the honest range is 4x to 40x, because judging models equal is a judgment call."

all.where: Visual 1 (particles) title: "The Convergence Dial: the race that keeps the umbrella up"; Visual 1 note: "the umbrella could lift because buyers slow down"; Visual 6 note: "the umbrella most likely holds through 2027"
all.why_opaque: This is the organising image of the entire section and it appears in a chart TITLE with no gloss. The only place on the page it is ever named is a chapter-1 chart note, six sections earlier, and even there it is a naming rather than a definition ("the list price sits roughly 7x above the cost to serve. Thompson calls this the price umbrella") — the referent is a pronoun in the previous sentence. A reader who skipped that one chart footnote has no idea what object is being kept "up", "lifted" or "held". Worse, the metaphor is directionally confusing: an umbrella going up sounds like a bad thing, but here it means the seller's margin survives. Every word is one or two syllables, so the readability gate sees nothing.
all.fix: Gloss it at the section's own first mention, in point 1, so the chart title lands: change "the extra margin should melt away" to "the extra margin, the price umbrella, should melt away." One clause, idea untouched.

all.where: Visual 5 note: "its CEO said the binding problem was power and shells, not chips sitting in inventory"
all.why_opaque: "Shells" is data-centre construction jargon for the physical buildings. A general reader has no candidate meaning at all here — shells of what? The nearest thing to a gloss anywhere on the page is chapter 4's "land, shells, power and network gear... A concrete shed and a power line last fifteen years or more", which never actually says shells are buildings and is three sections away. This is the purest example of the class the gate is blind to: one syllable, common word, industry-specific sense, and it sits in the sentence that carries the section's causal claim (the constraint is not chips).
all.fix: "...the binding problem was power and shells, the buildings that house the machines, not chips sitting in inventory."

all.where: Visual 3 (diverging) series sublabel, OpenAI o3 bar: "Jun 2025: $10/$40 → $2/$8 per M tokens, attributed to inference-stack optimisation"
all.why_opaque: Three pieces of unexplained machinery in one phrase: "inference" (running a trained model to produce an answer), "stack" (the layers of software around it), and the nominalised "optimisation". Nowhere on the page is "inference stack" glossed — chapter 3 only quotes OpenAI saying "We optimized our inference stack". This is an unforced error, because point 4 already renders the same fact perfectly in plain words ("said only the serving software had improved"); the label reverts to jargon on the single most load-bearing bar in the section, the one the note calls "the proof".
all.fix: "...attributed to better serving software, the code that runs the model, not a new model."

all.term: sticker (flagship sticker, frontier stickers, "Frontier sticker, trough to now")
all.where: Point 4: "The flagship sticker rose about four times over"; Visual 2 series label: "Frontier sticker, trough to now"; Visual 3 note: "it is sneakier than the sticker" and "the roughly 4× flagship sticker"
all.why_opaque: "Sticker" standing alone (not even "sticker price") is American car-dealership idiom for the published price before discounts. Chapters 1, 3 and 6 consistently use the plain term "list price"; chapter 7 switches to "sticker" without ever connecting the two, so the reader cannot tell whether a sticker is the same thing as a price, a rate, or a bill. It matters because the section's whole 2026 argument turns on the difference between the advertised sticker and what a customer actually pays. Two syllables, zero readability signal.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in point 4: "The flagship sticker, the published price before discounts, rose about four times over."

all.where: Point 4: "quieter changes pushed bills up even where the headline rate held still"; Visual 3 series sublabel: "at an unchanged headline rate"; Visual 3 note: "the headline rate did not move, the bill did"
all.why_opaque: Finance-journalism jargon for the advertised number as opposed to the realised one. The reader must already hold the headline/realised distinction to parse the sentence, and the sentence is the payoff of the whole 2026 reversal (the bill rose without the advertised price moving). Nothing on the page defines it; chapter 5's "headline run-rate" is equally unglossed. All short common words, so the gate passes it.
all.fix: Gloss at first use in point 4: "...pushed bills up even where the headline rate, the advertised price per token, held still."

all.where: Point 3: "An open marketplace routed 25.5 trillion tokens a week"; Point 5: "which take about 45 percent of routed tokens"; Visual 4 series label: "OpenRouter tokens routed per week"
all.why_opaque: "Routing" here means a broker passing a buyer's request on to whichever model they picked, and "routed tokens" means specifically the traffic through that one marketplace. Neither is explained. In point 5 this is not just opaque, it is actively misleading: a reader meets "45 percent of routed tokens" with no antecedent (point 3's marketplace is two paragraphs back and unnamed) and will naturally read it as 45 percent of all AI usage worldwide, which would be a much stronger claim than the evidence supports.
all.fix: In point 5, name the referent in the same clause: "...have left for Chinese open-weight models, which take about 45 percent of the tokens passing through that marketplace."

all.where: Visual 2 note: "The flagship figure is a hard read off official price cards: $1.25 to $5.00 per million input tokens"
all.why_opaque: Exactly the "rate card" failure mode: two short common words that are not standard English in combination and that appear nowhere else on the page (the rest of the piece says "list price" or "posted numbers"). A reader guesses at something between a menu and a loyalty card. It is doing evidential work here — the point is that this number is directly observable rather than estimated — so a vague read weakens the argument.
all.fix: Say it plainly: "a hard read off the labs' official published price lists" — no gloss needed once the phrase is ordinary.

all.term: input tokens / completion tokens, and the "$10/$40 per M tokens" pair notation
all.where: Visual 2 note: "$1.25 to $5.00 per million input tokens", "OpenAI $5/M input", "Anthropic's new tier above Opus at $10/M input"; Visual 3 sublabels: "$10/$40 → $2/$8 per M tokens" and "$15/$75 → $5/$25 per M tokens"; Visual 3 note: "the new model emits fewer completion tokens on long prompts"
all.why_opaque: The page defines "token" well (chapter 1: "a chunk of text, a bit under a word") but never tells the reader that labs bill text sent in and text sent back at two different rates. So the paired notation "$10/$40" is unreadable — the reader cannot tell if it is a range, a before/after, or a fraction — and "input tokens" versus "completion tokens" reads as two unrelated things. This matters because the 64 percent result depends entirely on output tokens falling while the input rate doubled.
all.fix: Add the key in the first sublabel that uses it — "$10/$40 → $2/$8 per million tokens (text in / text out)" — and in the note write "emits fewer completion tokens, the text it sends back, on long prompts."

all.where: Visual 6 note: "the median US interconnection wait has risen from under 20 months in 2005 to about 55 months for the 2023 cohort"
all.why_opaque: "Interconnection" is utility-industry jargon for the queue to get a new facility connected to the grid; "cohort" is research jargon for the projects that applied in a given year. This is the densest sentence in the section for a lay reader, and it is avoidable — the same note used the plain phrase "hookup requests" two sentences earlier and then switched registers. The sentence carries the mechanism behind the section's timing call (why supply cannot catch up quickly).
all.fix: Reuse the note's own plain phrase: "the median US wait to hook up to the grid has risen from under 20 months in 2005 to about 55 months for projects that applied in 2023."

all.where: Standfirst: "once compute catches up"; Point 1: "Answering each question burns compute", "because compute is scarce"; Point 5: "OpenAI's compute plan to 2030"; Visual 1 series label: "Supply: installed AI compute"
all.why_opaque: "Compute" as a mass noun meaning chips-plus-data-centre-capacity is insider usage; to a general reader compute is a verb, so "burns compute" and "compute is scarce" parse as errors before they parse as meaning. It is never glossed anywhere on the page. Mitigating: by chapter 7 the reader has met it repeatedly in context, and Visual 1's sublabel ("Global stock of AI chip compute") half-explains it — but the standfirst is a re-entry point where a reader may land cold.
all.fix: One clause in the standfirst: "...should sink toward the cost of running it once compute, the chips and data centres that run the models, catches up."

all.where: Point 5: "The gap is not closing. It is sorting."
all.why_opaque: "Sorting" is used in the economist's sense of a market separating into segments, and it is given no object — sorting what, into what? The reader has just been handed two percentages (45 percent of routed tokens, 67 percent of business spending) and the sentence is meant to be the interpretation of them, but as written it is a three-word sentence carrying an unstated technical idea. Four letters and two syllables, so no formula will ever flag it.
all.fix: Complete the clause rather than cut it: "It is sorting: price-led buyers into one market, business buyers into the other."

all.term: labs (as in "Top US labs", "the labs cut prices")
all.where: Point 1: "Top US labs charge far above that cost"; Point 4: "In 2025 the labs cut prices hard"
all.why_opaque: Industry shorthand for the handful of firms that build and sell frontier models. A reader with no background hears "lab" as a research institution, which quietly undercuts the argument — the whole point of points 1 and 4 is that these are profit-seeking sellers setting prices above cost, not researchers. The word is used this way from chapter 1 onward and is never glossed.
all.fix: Gloss once, at first use in point 1: "Top US labs, the firms that build and sell the best models, charge far above that cost."

all.term: grade A / grade B and the claim-id codes (sd-16, px-12, px-13, sd-06, sd-07)
all.where: Visual 1 note: "(see sd-16, OpenAI's 2030 compute plan...)"; Visual 2 note: "OpenAI $5/M input (px-13, grade A)"; Visual 5 note: "Google's cloud backlog at $514bn (sd-06, grade A)"
all.why_opaque: Not domain jargon but house notation, and it fails the same way: reader-visible strings that carry no meaning without a key. "see sd-16" instructs the reader to look somewhere with no indication of where, and "grade A" implies a rating scale that is never shown. A curious reader stops and hunts for a legend that is not on the page.
all.fix: Either drop the codes from reader-visible notes, or name the scale once per section on first use: "(grade A, meaning a directly published figure rather than an estimate)".

all.where: Visual 1 (diverging, "Does the whole program pay? Three cash-flow models") — all three series sublabels: "WACC 11% · 32% margin…", "WACC 9.5%…", "WACC 8.5%…"
all.why_opaque: The acronym is never expanded anywhere on the page — not in ch8, not in chapters 1-7. The prose does define the idea in plain words ("the price of the money - about nine or ten cents a year on each dollar") but never attaches that phrase to the four letters, so a reader meeting "WACC 11%" in a chart has no way to connect it to anything they just read. The chapter's own plain_check claims WACC was renamed away; the charts still ship it raw.
all.fix: Name it once where the plain definition already sits, in point 2: "the price of the money (WACC) - about nine or ten cents a year on each dollar".

all.where: Visual 1 (diverging) — series sublabels: "IRR 4%", "IRR 12.6% · $1.11 back per $1", "IRR 17.9%"
all.why_opaque: Never expanded or explained anywhere on the page.
