undefinedOnes.fix: Define the unit once and drop the model code: "It is 2.788 million GPU-hours — one chip running for one hour — at $2 each", and "roughly 50,000 Nvidia Hopper chips".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 5 note, final sentence: "Most of the US-China price gap is a scarcity premium collected on the American side."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Premium" in the pricing sense — an amount charged above cost — is never defined, and the word's dominant everyday meaning is quality (premium product, premium seat). A reader who takes that sense inverts the chapter's conclusion from "Americans can charge more because chips are scarce" into "American models are better, so they cost more", which is the exact reading the chapter spends five points dismantling. This sentence is the chapter's verdict, so the misread is expensive. Chapter 3's "pricing power here is scarcity, not greed" is helpful but sits three chapters back and uses different words.
undefinedOnes.fix: One clause: "a scarcity premium — extra charged simply because chips are hard to get — collected on the American side".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 note: "Matched-quality US-to-China ratio is about 10x, but the honest range is 4x to 40x (ce-17, grade C), because matched quality is a judgment call." Related sublabel: "China, open weights, matched to Sonnet 4.6".
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: A four-word noun pile built from a term of art. "Matched quality" means models judged to be about equally capable, and the ratio is of prices — but neither the comparison nor its direction is stated, so the reader must reverse-engineer that the claim is "for models of similar ability, the US price is roughly ten times the Chinese one". The trailing clause explains why the number is uncertain without ever saying what the number is.
undefinedOnes.fix: Say it as a sentence: "Compare models of similar ability and the US price is about 10x the Chinese one, though the honest range is 4x to 40x, because judging models equal is a judgment call."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 (particles) title: "The Convergence Dial: the race that keeps the umbrella up"; Visual 1 note: "the umbrella could lift because buyers slow down"; Visual 6 note: "the umbrella most likely holds through 2027"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: This is the organising image of the entire section and it appears in a chart TITLE with no gloss. The only place on the page it is ever named is a chapter-1 chart note, six sections earlier, and even there it is a naming rather than a definition ("the list price sits roughly 7x above the cost to serve. Thompson calls this the price umbrella") — the referent is a pronoun in the previous sentence. A reader who skipped that one chart footnote has no idea what object is being kept "up", "lifted" or "held". Worse, the metaphor is directionally confusing: an umbrella going up sounds like a bad thing, but here it means the seller's margin survives. Every word is one or two syllables, so the readability gate sees nothing.
undefinedOnes.fix: Gloss it at the section's own first mention, in point 1, so the chart title lands: change "the extra margin should melt away" to "the extra margin, the price umbrella, should melt away." One clause, idea untouched.

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 5 note: "its CEO said the binding problem was power and shells, not chips sitting in inventory"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Shells" is data-centre construction jargon for the physical buildings. A general reader has no candidate meaning at all here — shells of what? The nearest thing to a gloss anywhere on the page is chapter 4's "land, shells, power and network gear... A concrete shed and a power line last fifteen years or more", which never actually says shells are buildings and is three sections away. This is the purest example of the class the gate is blind to: one syllable, common word, industry-specific sense, and it sits in the sentence that carries the section's causal claim (the constraint is not chips).
undefinedOnes.fix: "...the binding problem was power and shells, the buildings that house the machines, not chips sitting in inventory."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 3 (diverging) series sublabel, OpenAI o3 bar: "Jun 2025: $10/$40 → $2/$8 per M tokens, attributed to inference-stack optimisation"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Three pieces of unexplained machinery in one phrase: "inference" (running a trained model to produce an answer), "stack" (the layers of software around it), and the nominalised "optimisation". Nowhere on the page is "inference stack" glossed — chapter 3 only quotes OpenAI saying "We optimized our inference stack". This is an unforced error, because point 4 already renders the same fact perfectly in plain words ("said only the serving software had improved"); the label reverts to jargon on the single most load-bearing bar in the section, the one the note calls "the proof".
undefinedOnes.fix: "...attributed to better serving software, the code that runs the model, not a new model."

undefinedOnes.term: sticker (flagship sticker, frontier stickers, "Frontier sticker, trough to now")
undefinedOnes.where: Point 4: "The flagship sticker rose about four times over"; Visual 2 series label: "Frontier sticker, trough to now"; Visual 3 note: "it is sneakier than the sticker" and "the roughly 4× flagship sticker"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Sticker" standing alone (not even "sticker price") is American car-dealership idiom for the published price before discounts. Chapters 1, 3 and 6 consistently use the plain term "list price"; chapter 7 switches to "sticker" without ever connecting the two, so the reader cannot tell whether a sticker is the same thing as a price, a rate, or a bill. It matters because the section's whole 2026 argument turns on the difference between the advertised sticker and what a customer actually pays. Two syllables, zero readability signal.
undefinedOnes.fix: Gloss at first use in point 4: "The flagship sticker, the published price before discounts, rose about four times over."

undefinedOnes.where: Point 4: "quieter changes pushed bills up even where the headline rate held still"; Visual 3 series sublabel: "at an unchanged headline rate"; Visual 3 note: "the headline rate did not move, the bill did"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Finance-journalism jargon for the advertised number as opposed to the realised one. The reader must already hold the headline/realised distinction to parse the sentence, and the sentence is the payoff of the whole 2026 reversal (the bill rose without the advertised price moving). Nothing on the page defines it; chapter 5's "headline run-rate" is equally unglossed. All short common words, so the gate passes it.
undefinedOnes.fix: Gloss at first use in point 4: "...pushed bills up even where the headline rate, the advertised price per token, held still."

undefinedOnes.where: Point 3: "An open marketplace routed 25.5 trillion tokens a week"; Point 5: "which take about 45 percent of routed tokens"; Visual 4 series label: "OpenRouter tokens routed per week"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Routing" here means a broker passing a buyer's request on to whichever model they picked, and "routed tokens" means specifically the traffic through that one marketplace. Neither is explained. In point 5 this is not just opaque, it is actively misleading: a reader meets "45 percent of routed tokens" with no antecedent (point 3's marketplace is two paragraphs back and unnamed) and will naturally read it as 45 percent of all AI usage worldwide, which would be a much stronger claim than the evidence supports.
undefinedOnes.fix: In point 5, name the referent in the same clause: "...have left for Chinese open-weight models, which take about 45 percent of the tokens passing through that marketplace."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 2 note: "The flagship figure is a hard read off official price cards: $1.25 to $5.00 per million input tokens"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Exactly the "rate card" failure mode: two short common words that are not standard English in combination and that appear nowhere else on the page (the rest of the piece says "list price" or "posted numbers"). A reader guesses at something between a menu and a loyalty card. It is doing evidential work here — the point is that this number is directly observable rather than estimated — so a vague read weakens the argument.
undefinedOnes.fix: Say it plainly: "a hard read off the labs' official published price lists" — no gloss needed once the phrase is ordinary.

undefinedOnes.term: input tokens / completion tokens, and the "$10/$40 per M tokens" pair notation
undefinedOnes.where: Visual 2 note: "$1.25 to $5.00 per million input tokens", "OpenAI $5/M input", "Anthropic's new tier above Opus at $10/M input"; Visual 3 sublabels: "$10/$40 → $2/$8 per M tokens" and "$15/$75 → $5/$25 per M tokens"; Visual 3 note: "the new model emits fewer completion tokens on long prompts"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The page defines "token" well (chapter 1: "a chunk of text, a bit under a word") but never tells the reader that labs bill text sent in and text sent back at two different rates. So the paired notation "$10/$40" is unreadable — the reader cannot tell if it is a range, a before/after, or a fraction — and "input tokens" versus "completion tokens" reads as two unrelated things. This matters because the 64 percent result depends entirely on output tokens falling while the input rate doubled.
undefinedOnes.fix: Add the key in the first sublabel that uses it — "$10/$40 → $2/$8 per million tokens (text in / text out)" — and in the note write "emits fewer completion tokens, the text it sends back, on long prompts."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 6 note: "the median US interconnection wait has risen from under 20 months in 2005 to about 55 months for the 2023 cohort"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Interconnection" is utility-industry jargon for the queue to get a new facility connected to the grid; "cohort" is research jargon for the projects that applied in a given year. This is the densest sentence in the section for a lay reader, and it is avoidable — the same note used the plain phrase "hookup requests" two sentences earlier and then switched registers. The sentence carries the mechanism behind the section's timing call (why supply cannot catch up quickly).
undefinedOnes.fix: Reuse the note's own plain phrase: "the median US wait to hook up to the grid has risen from under 20 months in 2005 to about 55 months for projects that applied in 2023."

undefinedOnes.where: Standfirst: "once compute catches up"; Point 1: "Answering each question burns compute", "because compute is scarce"; Point 5: "OpenAI's compute plan to 2030"; Visual 1 series label: "Supply: installed AI compute"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Compute" as a mass noun meaning chips-plus-data-centre-capacity is insider usage; to a general reader compute is a verb, so "burns compute" and "compute is scarce" parse as errors before they parse as meaning. It is never glossed anywhere on the page. Mitigating: by chapter 7 the reader has met it repeatedly in context, and Visual 1's sublabel ("Global stock of AI chip compute") half-explains it — but the standfirst is a re-entry point where a reader may land cold.
undefinedOnes.fix: One clause in the standfirst: "...should sink toward the cost of running it once compute, the chips and data centres that run the models, catches up."

undefinedOnes.where: Point 5: "The gap is not closing. It is sorting."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Sorting" is used in the economist's sense of a market separating into segments, and it is given no object — sorting what, into what? The reader has just been handed two percentages (45 percent of routed tokens, 67 percent of business spending) and the sentence is meant to be the interpretation of them, but as written it is a three-word sentence carrying an unstated technical idea. Four letters and two syllables, so no formula will ever flag it.
undefinedOnes.fix: Complete the clause rather than cut it: "It is sorting: price-led buyers into one market, business buyers into the other."

undefinedOnes.term: labs (as in "Top US labs", "the labs cut prices")
undefinedOnes.where: Point 1: "Top US labs charge far above that cost"; Point 4: "In 2025 the labs cut prices hard"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Industry shorthand for the handful of firms that build and sell frontier models. A reader with no background hears "lab" as a research institution, which quietly undercuts the argument — the whole point of points 1 and 4 is that these are profit-seeking sellers setting prices above cost, not researchers. The word is used this way from chapter 1 onward and is never glossed.
undefinedOnes.fix: Gloss once, at first use in point 1: "Top US labs, the firms that build and sell the best models, charge far above that cost."

undefinedOnes.term: grade A / grade B and the claim-id codes (sd-16, px-12, px-13, sd-06, sd-07)
undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 note: "(see sd-16, OpenAI's 2030 compute plan...)"; Visual 2 note: "OpenAI $5/M input (px-13, grade A)"; Visual 5 note: "Google's cloud backlog at $514bn (sd-06, grade A)"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Not domain jargon but house notation, and it fails the same way: reader-visible strings that carry no meaning without a key. "see sd-16" instructs the reader to look somewhere with no indication of where, and "grade A" implies a rating scale that is never shown. A curious reader stops and hunts for a legend that is not on the page.
undefinedOnes.fix: Either drop the codes from reader-visible notes, or name the scale once per section on first use: "(grade A, meaning a directly published figure rather than an estimate)".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 (diverging, "Does the whole program pay? Three cash-flow models") — all three series sublabels: "WACC 11% · 32% margin…", "WACC 9.5%…", "WACC 8.5%…"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The acronym is never expanded anywhere on the page — not in ch8, not in chapters 1-7. The prose does define the idea in plain words ("the price of the money - about nine or ten cents a year on each dollar") but never attaches that phrase to the four letters, so a reader meeting "WACC 11%" in a chart has no way to connect it to anything they just read. The chapter's own plain_check claims WACC was renamed away; the charts still ship it raw.
undefinedOnes.fix: Name it once where the plain definition already sits, in point 2: "the price of the money (WACC) - about nine or ten cents a year on each dollar".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 (diverging) — series sublabels: "IRR 4%", "IRR 12.6% · $1.11 back per $1", "IRR 17.9%"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Never expanded or explained anywhere on the page. Unlike WACC it has no plain-language cousin in the prose at all, so the reader gets three bare percentages with no idea what they measure or which direction is good. Worse, the reader cannot see that the whole verdict is IRR-vs-WACC: bear fails because 4% < 11%, base clears because 12.6% > 9.5%.
undefinedOnes.fix: Add one clause to the visual's note: "IRR is the yearly rate the money earns; it pays only when IRR beats the price of the money."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 (diverging) — unit: "USD billions, net present value"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The reader is asked to read signed billions where the sign IS the finding (bear -2,300 fails, base +487 clears), but nothing tells them that this number is already net of the cost of the money, so zero is the pass line. Without that, -$2.3T reads as "loses $2.3 trillion of cash" rather than "falls $2.3 trillion short of the bar" — a different and much stronger claim.
undefinedOnes.fix: Add one clause to the note: "Net present value is today's worth of all the future cash after charging for the price of the money - above zero means it pays."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 1 (diverging) — series labels "Bear", "Base", "Bull" and note ("Bear fails; base and bull clear… base-to-bear is a $2.8T fall while base-to-bull is only a $0.4T rise")
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Every syllable-counting test waves these through, but they are finance jargon, and the chapter deliberately uses a second, plainer vocabulary in the prose ("the glum model", "the middle", "the sunny") and in visual 4 ("Glum model assumes", "Middle model assumes", "Sunny model assumes"). The reader must silently learn that bear=glum and bull=sunny with nothing on the page saying so, and must do it while reading the chapter's single most important chart.
undefinedOnes.fix: Relabel the series to carry both: "Glum (bear)", "Middle (base)", "Sunny (bull)".

undefinedOnes.where: Point 5 ("though a short-seller claims the group hides $176 billion of wear") and visual 5 note ("yet a short-seller claims the group hides $176B of wear across 2026-2028")
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The sentence is built as a caveat-on-a-caveat, and the only thing that tells the reader how much weight to give the $176B is who is making the claim. A reader who does not know a short-seller is paid when the price falls loses the entire reason the sentence says "claims" rather than "shows".
undefinedOnes.fix: "though a short-seller - an investor who profits if the shares fall - claims the group hides $176 billion of wear".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 7 (particles) — note ("This is the odds the bet clears its cost of capital") and series label ("odds it clears cost of capital")
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: This is the closing image of the chapter and it introduces a third name for a thing already named twice: "the price of the money" in the prose and "WACC" in the charts. Nothing links the three. The reader arrives at the payoff moment and is asked to accept that 52% is the odds of clearing a bar they may not recognise as the bar they were shown earlier.
undefinedOnes.fix: "the odds the bet clears its cost of capital - that price of money, about 9.5 cents a year on each dollar".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 7 (particles) — note: "the rest cool and fall into the write-down reservoir"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Short, common-looking, and never defined on the page. The reader can tell from "cool and fall" that it is the bad outcome, but not what actually happens - that the owner formally admits the asset is worth less than the books say, which is the exact mechanism the chip-life argument in point 5 is driving at.
undefinedOnes.fix: "fall into the write-down reservoir - value the owners have admitted is gone".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 3 (dot_spread) — series label "Outside-view" and note ("three lenses (outside-view, valuation, contrarian)")
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: A term of art from forecasting, not ordinary English, and the label is doing real work: the note's claim that three independent lenses converge is only persuasive if the reader knows the lenses differ in method. "Outside-view" reads to a general reader as "an outsider's opinion" - the opposite of its actual meaning (scoring this case by how the class of similar past cases turned out).
undefinedOnes.fix: Relabel to "Outside-view (scored by how similar past build-outs turned out)" and leave the other two labels as they are.

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 3 (dot_spread) — series label "Valuation (DCF)"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Never expanded anywhere on the page. The parenthesis is presumably there to tell the reader how this panelist reached 0.53, so an unreadable acronym costs the label its whole function.
undefinedOnes.fix: Relabel to "Valuation (discounted cash flow)".

undefinedOnes.where: Point 2: "One house says near $2 trillion by 2030, short by roughly $800 billion."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Exactly the failure mode the readability gate cannot see: one syllable, everyday word, insider sense. In finance a "house" is a research or brokerage firm; to a general reader the sentence reads as a typo or as a household. It also sits in a run of three unattributed sources ("One rule says… One house says… A third sees…") where the reader is already working to keep the claims apart.
undefinedOnes.fix: "One research house - an analyst firm - says near $2 trillion by 2030".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 2 (comparison) note: "Log scale, because the gap is roughly 20x."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The note explains why a log scale was chosen but not what one is. A reader who does not know will compare the bars by length and badly under-read the gap - which is the chart's entire point - because $1,500B does not look 20x $71B on the page.
undefinedOnes.fix: "Log scale, where each step multiplies rather than adds, because the gap is roughly 20x."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 8 "Does the whole build pay? Three scenarios" — unit string: "USD billions (net present value)". It is the unit of the single most important chart in the piece.
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: NPV is never defined anywhere in the nine sections — it appears only as a bare unit label here and in chapter 8. A reader with no finance background sees "$487B" and "-$2,300B" and has no idea what quantity those are: profit? cash? spending? The whole verdict on the trillion-dollar build turns on a number whose meaning is never stated. Three short common words, so every readability formula waves it through.
undefinedOnes.fix: Gloss it in the note's opening sentence, which already sets up the calculation: "...discounted at a 9-10% cost of capital, giving a net present value — what all those future dollars are worth in today's money."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 8 note ("The hinge is the mature margin — about 5c either way moves the base case roughly $0.5T") and all three series sublabels: "32c mature margin", "43c mature margin", "55c mature margin".
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The note itself calls this the hinge of the entire answer, and the compound is never glossed. "Mature" is doing real work — it means the margin the industry settles at once it stops growing, not today's margin — and a reader cannot recover that from "mature". Worse, chapter 5 defined margin as a share of a revenue dollar, so "32c mature margin" reads as a different unit again with no bridge. Two everyday words; formula-invisible.
undefinedOnes.fix: At first use in the note: "the mature margin (the cents of each sales dollar the industry keeps once it is grown up)".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 9 note "The honest answer is a coin toss": "Will the total US AI build — all vintages plus the tail — earn back its cost of capital?"
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Only appearance of the word on the entire page. In capital analysis a vintage is the batch of money committed in a given year; to a general reader it means wine, or possibly "old". It sits in the framing clause of the headline question, so a reader who mis-parses it mis-parses what the 52% is about. Chapter 8 said the same thing in plain words ("one batch of chips", "every dollar from 2024 to 2030"); chapter 9 swaps in the jargon.
undefinedOnes.fix: "all vintages (every year's batch of spending) plus the tail".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 8 note, first sentence: "...plus a tail for the years beyond, discounted at a 9-10% cost of capital."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "Discount" appears elsewhere on the page only in its shop sense (chapter 6, "DeepSeek off-peak discount"), so a reader will import the wrong meaning — that the cash flows were marked down or cut. The financial sense (future dollars converted to today's money at a rate) is the mechanical core of the whole payback answer and is never stated. Common word, two syllables; invisible to FK, Fog and SMOG.
undefinedOnes.fix: "discounted — future dollars marked back to what they are worth today — at a 9-10% cost of capital".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 3 note "Chinese price is a strategy dial, not a cost floor (T3)": "its own disclosed data implied a 545% theoretical margin (cd-04), not a firm selling at cost."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: This is worse than undefined: it collides with the page's own definition. Chapter 5 taught the reader that margin is "the share of each revenue dollar left after the direct cost of serving it" — a quantity that cannot exceed 100%. A reader who learned that definition reads 545% as a typo or gives up. The figure is a markup over cost, a different measure wearing the same word, and nothing signals the switch.
undefinedOnes.fix: Bind the sense at use: "a 545% theoretical margin (a markup over its own serving cost, not a share of the sales dollar)".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 8 note ("discounted at a 9-10% cost of capital"), Visual 9 note ("earn back its cost of capital"), and Visual 9 unit string ("% probability the whole build clears its cost of capital").
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Point 5 glosses the idea well — "ask if it earns back more than that money could earn elsewhere" — but never attaches the label to the gloss, so the three later bare uses arrive as an unexplained term. Chapter 8 glossed it differently again ("the price of the money"), so the reader has two unnamed paraphrases and one un-glossed name. It is the unit of the piece's headline number, which makes the loose binding expensive.
undefinedOnes.fix: Bind it once, in point 5: "...and ask if it earns back more than that money could earn elsewhere — its cost of capital." Then the later bare uses land.

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 8 note ("plus a tail for the years beyond"), Visual 9 note ("all vintages plus the tail"), Visual 10 note ("It is why the whole case rests on the tail"); the idea also carries point 5.
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: "A tail for the years beyond" is a half-gloss: it tells the reader the tail is later years, but not that it is a single lumped estimate of everything after the model's horizon — the terminal-value assumption that the entire positive verdict depends on. By Visual 10 ("the whole case rests on the tail") the phrase is being used as a load-bearing noun the reader has never been given. Chapter 8 also left it undefined ("the whole payoff hides in a long tail").
undefinedOnes.fix: At first use: "plus a tail (one lumped estimate for all the years after 2030)".

undefinedOnes.where: Point 2 ("US list prices sit far above serving cost") and Visual 2 note ("serving is about 15% of US list price"; "scarcity keeps list prices up").
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Never defined in any of the nine sections, yet the entire T2 verdict is the gap between list price and serving cost. A general reader half-knows it from car showrooms but will not be sure whether it means the posted price, the price anyone actually pays, or the price after enterprise discounts — and that ambiguity is exactly what the claim hinges on. Two of the most common words in English; no formula will ever flag it.
undefinedOnes.fix: In point 2: "US list prices — the posted price, before any deal — sit far above serving cost".

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 6 note "Supply is coming — the money is pledged (T5)": "Each bar carries its 80% range." Also "its 80% whisker" in the same visual's rationale text (visible under "why this chart").
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The only explanation on the page is the footer's "Shaded bands are 80% confidence intervals" — which sits after every use and swaps one piece of jargon for another. A reader does not know whether the 80% range means eight in ten past cases, an 80% chance of landing inside, or a margin of error. Chapter 8 had the good plain gloss ("would-not-be-shocked ranges") and chapter 9 drops it.
undefinedOnes.fix: "Each bar carries its 80% range — the band we would not be shocked to see it land in."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 5 note "The claim with the money on it moved the wrong way (T5)", final sentence: "The umbrella leaks; it does not break."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: The closing line of the section's pivotal chart is a metaphor callback with no antecedent the reader can use. Chapter 1 only names it ("Thompson calls this the price umbrella") and chapter 3's eyebrow repeats the name; nowhere is it said what the umbrella IS — the gap between price and cost that scarcity holds open. Chapter 9 then drops even the word "price", so it arrives as a bare noun several screens after its only mention.
undefinedOnes.fix: "The price umbrella — the gap above cost that scarcity holds open — leaks; it does not break."

undefinedOnes.where: Visual 8 note, closing line: "Figures from the P1 total-program DCF model; not an externally graded claim."
undefinedOnes.why_opaque: Unexpanded acronym, first and only expansion nowhere on the page (chapter 8 uses it the same way, as a bare label "Valuation (DCF)").
